title: Springfield Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Springfield wells have a 170 ft median depth; see local yields, water levels, drilling costs, risks and permit history.
h1: Springfield, Colorado Well Depth, Yield and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land near Springfield means looking past the listing and into the well records. Within 5 miles of Springfield in Baca County, Colorado DWR records show 413 permitted wells, with 186 recorded as constructed. The available records point to a generally productive plains setting, but individual results still vary by location, aquifer and construction.

The local numbers are useful for budgeting and screening a property. They are not a guarantee for a new hole. A buyer should confirm the permit, well construction, measured water level, pump information and neighboring wells before relying on a domestic or livestock water source.

sections.heading: Springfield well depths vary across the plains
sections.html:
The median recorded well depth near Springfield is 170 feet. The middle half runs from 105 to 300 feet, so a driller bidding a typical site may need to plan for substantially more than the median. One-quarter of the depth records are between 300 and 600 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 740 feet.

Depth records are split across the local plains geology: 23% are under 100 feet, 52% are 100 to 300 feet, 25% are 300 to 600 feet, and 1% are deeper than 600 feet. Permits name unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers most often, followed by the Dakota and Southern High Plains aquifers. There are no Denver Basin aquifer wells in these records.

sections.heading: What Springfield wells produce
sections.html:
Among the 61 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 50.0 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 15.0 to 400.0 gallons per minute, which is a wide spread and a reminder that one neighbor's result does not establish another property's supply.

The yield mix is favorable on paper: 82% report more than 15 gallons per minute, 16% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 2% report less than 1 gallon per minute. Only 61 wells report yield, however, compared with 413 permitted wells. For a home buyer, storage and pump testing still matter, especially if the intended use includes livestock, irrigation or more than ordinary household demand.

sections.heading: Water levels near Springfield and the recorded trend
sections.html:
The median static water level is 39 feet below ground surface, with the middle half from 20 to 95 feet. That is the depth to standing water when a well is not being pumped, not the total well depth. It helps a contractor think about pump setting, trenching and the water column, but the measurement from the specific property is more useful than the area median.

By measurement decade, the median was 20 feet below surface in the 2010s and 64 feet in the 2020s. That shift suggests deeper measured water levels in the newer decade, but it does not by itself prove a uniform regional water-table decline. Different wells, aquifers, seasons and measurement methods can affect the comparison.

sections.heading: Springfield permit history and local drillers
sections.html:
Permit activity stretches back to the 1950s, when 7 permits were issued. The busiest recorded decade was the 1970s with 74 permits, followed by 51 in the 2000s, 49 in the 2010s, and 31 in the 2020s. The newest permit year in the records is 2025. Use categories are 31% domestic or household, 24% stock, 28% irrigation and 16% monitoring.

The most active named drillers in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 44 wells; Ogden Drilling (Ogden Jr., Arthur F.), with 36; and Konkel Drilling (Konkel, David Leroy), with 22. These counts describe permit records, not current availability or a recommendation. Colorado DWR permit and construction documents should be checked for the property being bought.

sections.heading: What a new Springfield well may cost
sections.html:
For alluvium and plains sedimentary rock near Springfield, the drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 170-foot median depth, the drilled hole models to about $6,000 to $9,400. That is only the hole, not a complete operating water system.

A finished well including pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $12,000 to $21,400 at the median depth. A site requiring a 300-foot or deeper hole can move beyond that range, while a shallower site may cost less. Get a written bid that separates drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, electrical, trenching and any difficult access or formation charges.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying or building
sections.html:
Low yield is not the dominant result in the reported Springfield sample, but dry holes and poor results remain possible because the records do not cover every property and fractured-bedrock conditions can be unpredictable. A 2% share of reported wells under 1 gallon per minute is a warning that very weak wells do exist. Ask for the actual well construction, pump yield and static-level records, not just a verbal claim.

There are 6 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites mapped within about 10 miles. That does not establish contamination at a particular parcel, but it supports testing before purchase. Also check septic setbacks, available building area, drainage, access for a rig, and the relationship between the proposed septic system and the well. Water rights and augmentation requirements can matter in over-appropriated basins.

sections.heading: A practical plan for a Springfield lot
sections.html:
Start with the DWR permit number and confirm that the permitted use fits the home, stock or irrigation plan. Then compare nearby records in Springfield, Vilas, Pritchett and Two Buttes rather than relying on a single well. Look for construction depth, casing and grout, pump yield, static water level and the named aquifer. Records from Walsh, Campo and Kim can add regional context, but the closest comparable wells deserve the most weight.

Before closing, arrange an independent water-quality test and have a qualified contractor review the pump, pressure system, septic layout and access. For new construction, price the complete system instead of drilling alone. A Colorado exempt household-use well still has permit and use limits, and a 35 gallon-per-minute exempt-well pumping limit does not mean every local well can produce that amount.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Springfield, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within 5 miles of Springfield is 170 feet. The middle half runs from 105 to 300 feet, while the deepest record is 740 feet. About 52% of wells are 100 to 300 feet deep, but 25% reach 300 to 600 feet, so a site-specific estimate is still necessary.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Springfield, Colorado?
faq.a: The local drilling model is $35 to $55 per foot. At the 170-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $6,000 to $9,400. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $12,000 to $21,400. Greater depth, difficult access and formation conditions can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce near Springfield?
faq.a: Of the 61 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 50.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 15.0 to 400.0 gallons per minute. Reported results include 2% under 1 gallon per minute. Because only 61 wells report yield, buyers should verify the specific well and test the pump rather than rely on the area median.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Springfield, Colorado?
faq.a: The records map 6 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those locations do not prove a problem at your property. Test the well before purchase and after construction, including concerns identified by local environmental records. Review the well, septic and nearby land uses together.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping near Springfield, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded static water level was 20 feet below surface in the 2010s and 64 feet in the 2020s. That suggests deeper measured levels in the newer decade, but it does not prove a uniform water-table decline because the wells, aquifers, seasons and measurement conditions may differ. Check the property's own static-level history when available.
